focus: Governor Robert Hunter Morris's admitted love of disputation locks him into continual conflict with the Pennsylvania Assembly despite promising Franklin he would avoid it, and that conflict is traced to proprietary instructions shielding the Penn family's estates from taxation. When Morris blocks a wartime funding bill over that same exemption demand, Franklin sidesteps the governor entirely by having the Assembly issue an interest-bearing financial instrument instead of a tax.
coreClaim: Chronic disputes between Pennsylvania's governors and its Assembly stemmed from proprietary instructions protecting the Penn family's estates from taxation, and the way out of such a deadlock lay in engineering a financial instrument rather than winning the argument.

centralConcept.name: Loan-Office order financing
centralConcept.plainDefinition: A way of raising money for a public expense by having the Assembly issue interest-bearing paper drawn on the provincial loan office, instead of relying on a tax bill the governor could veto.
centralConcept.whyItMatters: It let a legislature fund an urgent commitment even when the executive refused consent, because it never required an act the governor had to sign.

keyClaims: Robert Hunter Morris arrived from England to replace Governor Hamilton, who had resigned worn out by disputes forced on him by his proprietary instructions.
Morris openly admitted enjoying disputation and predicted, accurately, that he would keep quarreling with the Assembly despite promising Franklin he would try to avoid it.
Habitual disputants may win individual arguments but generally forfeit the goodwill that would serve them better, a pattern Morris's upbringing at his father's dinner table had trained into him.
Franklin and Morris kept a warm personal friendship even while Franklin drafted the Assembly's harshest replies against him, showing institutional conflict need not become personal animosity.

A joking exchange about selling off an ungovernable people escalated into a public insult contest that damaged Morris's own reputation more than the Assembly's, and he eventually quit the post as Hamilton had.
The recurring governor-Assembly conflict was rooted in the Penn family's instructions binding their deputies by bond to block any tax act that did not exempt the proprietors' own estates.

When Morris refused assent to a Crown Point relief bill over that same tax exemption, Franklin devised interest-bearing Loan-Office orders that raised the needed money without the governor's signature, and the orders sold out within weeks as an attractive investment.

namedExamples.label: Massachusetts Bay's Crown Point appeal / Loan-Office orders funding Pennsylvania's ten-thousand-pound aid
namedExamples.summary: Massachusetts Bay sent Mr. Quincy to Pennsylvania seeking help for an attack on Crown Point, and Franklin, as Quincy's fellow New Englander and a sitting Assembly member, dictated the address that won the Assembly's vote of ten thousand pounds. Governor Morris refused to sign the funding bill unless the proprietary estate was exempted from the tax paying for it, so Franklin proposed issuing Loan-Office orders instead, letting the Assembly raise the money on its own authority. The orders sold out within weeks as an attractive investment, and Quincy went home with the aid secured and a lasting friendship with Franklin.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: A legislative deadlock created by an executive veto can sometimes be dissolved by inventing a new financial instrument rather than winning the underlying argument.

hardEdge: It is tempting to conclude that the endless quarrels between the Assembly and its governors were personal squabbles, driven by a contentious temperament like Morris's, and that a more agreeable governor could simply have avoided them. What actually holds is that the conflict was structural: the Penn family bound every deputy governor by bond to block any tax act that did not exempt their own estates, so no governor's personality could resolve it, and the deadlock only broke when a financial instrument was invented that never required the governor's assent at all — which is exactly what the personal-friction reading misses.

paraphraseNotes: Robert Hunter Morris arrived at New York from England to take over the Pennsylvania governorship from Hamilton, who had resigned exhausted by disputes his proprietary instructions forced on him. Franklin told Morris he could have a comfortable term if he simply avoided quarreling with the Assembly; Morris admitted he loved disputing, called it one of his greatest pleasures, and promised only to try avoiding it. His taste for argument traced back to a habit his own father had cultivated, setting his children against each other at the dinner table for entertainment — a training Franklin judged unwise, since people who habitually dispute and confute others may win arguments but permanently lose the goodwill that would serve them better. By the time Franklin returned from a trip to Boston, the Assembly's own records already showed Morris locked in a continual battle with the House that lasted his whole administration; Franklin himself sat on every committee assigned to answer Morris's messages and usually wrote the replies, which were often tart and sometimes indecently abusive. Despite this, the two men's personal friendship survived intact, and they often dined together. At one such dinner, Morris joked about admiring Sancho Panza's wish to govern only blacks so he could sell them if they proved troublesome; when a friend of Morris's needled Franklin for siding with the Quakers instead of selling them, Franklin retorted that the governor hadn't yet blackened them enough — a jab at Morris's own attempts to blacken the Assembly's reputation, attempts that rebounded onto him until, worn out, he quit the post as Hamilton had. The underlying cause of these clashes was structural: the Penn family bound its deputy governors by bond to block any tax act that did not exempt the proprietors' own vast estates, and the Assembly held out against this for three years before bending. When Morris blocked a ten-thousand-pound relief bill for the Crown Point expedition on that same exemption demand, Franklin sidestepped the governor entirely by having the Assembly issue interest-bearing Loan-Office orders, which sold out within weeks because they doubled as an attractive investment. The practical rule: when an executive veto is structurally guaranteed, invent a financial instrument that needs no veto, rather than trying to win an argument nobody in that seat is free to concede.

testableFacts.becauseMechanism: Proprietary instructions bound any governor to demands the Assembly resisted, so occupying the office meant inheriting the same forced conflict regardless of personal temperament.
testableFacts.commonError: Hamilton resigned because he personally disliked politics in general.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: The text ties his exhaustion specifically to disputes generated by his proprietary instructions, not to distaste for the job itself.

testableFacts.claim: Morris's repeated attempts to blacken the Assembly's reputation in his official messages were thrown back onto him, and he grew tired of the contest and quit, as Hamilton had before him.
